newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Australian retailers sidestep spending spree.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Australian retailers sidestep spending spree.

text.p: Australian consumers have emerged from the economic slowdown of 1996 and are opting to spend their spare money at restaurants, movie theatres and casinos rather than splashing out at the department store.

A new survey on retail spending behaviour released on Monday shows that consumers are choosing to spend the fruits of the recovery on entertainment and leisure rather than on new durable goods or clothes.
Analysts agreed this trend was strengthening.

Department stores and other traditional retailers are seen to be missing out as a new surge in consumption moves away from the struggling retailers who have long been wondering how to recapture customers.

"After a long period of enforced hibernation during the recession and the cautious years following it, consumers are once again enjoying that liberating feeling of spending," said Values Bank managing director Ross Honeywill.
"But significantly, this spend trend is centred on the need to reward themselves. It is about instant personal gratification," Honeywill said.

A survey of the spending patterns and behaviour of 1100 consumers by George Patterson Bates and The Values Bank Research Centre found spending on entertainment jumped 12 percent in the nine months to March 1997.
The survey found spending on food rose 10 percent while spending on discretionary goods fell 12 percent over the same period.

Australian Bureau of Statistics data for the first five months of 1997 also supports the trend. Food sales grew at an average rate of 0.4 percent a month and restaurant, hotel and cafe sales rose by an average 0.5 percent a month.
This compares with an average 0.35 percent fall per month in department store sales over that period.

Analysts said the trend away from apparel and durable goods to entertainment and leisure has been evident in recent years, but appeared to have strengthened in the last six months as discretionary spending recovered.
"Growth in some of the retail categories like clothing and household durables is at its lowest levels for 10 years," said Prudential-Bache retail analyst John Burgess.

Entertainment and other services spending had dropped off during the recession like everything else, but appeared to be bouncing back stronger once the recession was over, Burgess said. Consumers had enough durable goods and now wanted to use their time better and enjoy their leisure time more, he said.
"It's a combination of a time-poor lifestyle and an ageing population who tend to spend more on services," he said.
The George Patterson/Value survey meant retailers would have to change the way they sell things.
"People want experiences with their spending," said Values Bank Research Director Brent Taylor told Reuters.
"The best examples are retail outlets like Myer Sport," he said.

Coles Myer Ltd has tested a separate sporting goods operation within its Melbourne department store this year, offering hands-on experiences like golf driving ranges, basketball shooting galleries along with its sports goods sales.
Retail analysts said the concept appeared to have been successful and may prove the key to a recovery in the retail sector.

Stocks like department store group David Jones Ltd and Country Road Ltd have suffered in the last year as retail sales disappointed, while cinema operators like Hoyts Cinemas Ltd and the operator of Melbourne's casino, Crown Casino Ltd, have fared better.
